title: Mu
hookLine: a monk asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has Buddha-nature; he answers "mu" (Gateless Gate 1)
carry: see what's there before you pick a side

lines: A STRAY DOG IN THE COURTYARD.
cards: Northern China, more than a thousand years ago. A stray dog wanders through a monastery courtyard. A monk watches it and turns to the old teacher Zhaozhou with a question he's clearly been saving.
Does a dog have Buddha-nature, or not? The case doesn't say why he asks. But every monk there knew what the books said, so the question has a trap in it.
Zhaozhou gives him one syllable. Wu. In Japanese, mu.
It's the first case in the Gateless Gate, and for centuries it's been the first koan many Zen students are given.

teach.b: Here's why the answer is so strange. Mahayana sutras teach that all living beings have Buddha-nature, the capacity to wake up. So the textbook answer is yes.
And mu means no. Or not, or without, or nothing. In one breath, it seems, Zhaozhou contradicted the scriptures.
Argue that he meant no, and you're stuck. Argue that he meant yes, and you're stuck.
Wumen, the monk who compiled the Gateless Gate in 1228, says in his comment that mu isn't the no of yes and no, and it isn't the nothing of being and nothing.
Work on it with your whole body, he says, day and night, like someone who has swallowed a red-hot iron ball and can't spit it out. Tradition says Wumen himself worked on mu for six years.
Here's a detail most people never hear.
In another collection, the Book of Serenity, the same question comes to Zhaozhou on another day, and that time he answers: yes.
Many teachers read it as a sign the answer was never the point; what mattered was what was happening in the person who asked.

Zhaozhou, by tradition, lived to about one hundred twenty, teaching into extreme old age, well-known for plain words that stopped people in their tracks. Mu is his most well-known one. Students don't explain it.
They become it, breath by breath.

how: In Rinzai Zen and some Western Zen communities, 'mu' is often the first koan a teacher assigns; students breathe with it in sitting meditation and bring their response to private interviews with the teacher.

o: a short Japanese word for a stray or homeless dog
a sacred sound chanted to open every Zen sitting
Zhaozhou's one-word reply that cuts off both yes and no

games.q: match each piece of the first koan.

s: Zhaozhou's 'mu' simply means dogs lack Buddha-nature
Wumen says it isn't the no of yes and no.
Mahayana sutras teach that all beings have Buddha-nature
that's why the monk's question was a trap.
in another collection Zhaozhou answers the same question with yes
the Book of Serenity records both answers.

games.q: you're Zhaozhou. a monk asks whether a dog has Buddha-nature, a question he already knows the textbook answer to. what do you say?
o: quote the sutra: yes, all beings have it.
give a long talk on Buddha-nature.
games.why: Zhaozhou said 'wu', mu in Japanese, which cut off both the textbook yes and any clever no.

practice: On each out-breath, let the sound mu go out with it, silently or as the softest hum, not thinking about what it means, just the sound riding the breath all the way out. When a thought comes, let the next mu follow it.
If you'd like, imagine the sound filling the whole body, head to feet.

wordCard.voice: Mu. Zhaozhou's one-syllable answer about the dog: no, not, nothing, and none of those. The first koan of the Gateless Gate.

orig.note: Japanese mu, Chinese wú: no, not, without, nothing.

carryVoice: Your line: see what's there before you pick a side. Not the yes, not the no: mu. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), case 1 and Wumen's comment
